analysis.one_liner: Sets the first federal safety standards for underground natural gas storage facilities, funded by operator fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 19 Democratic cosponsors, but it never got a committee vote or floor action and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill directed the Department of Transportation to write the first minimum federal safety standards for underground natural gas storage facilities within 180 days, and immediately required every facility to meet interim requirements, including industry recommended practices and recommendations in a safety advisory the pipeline regulator issued on February 2, 2016. It funded research on storage safety and a fully detectable, nontoxic odorant for gas, and charged each storage operator a user fee to pay for the oversight. The bill came from California House Democrats, whose constituents had just lived through the Aliso Canyon storage leak near Los Angeles, and it stalled in subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near underground gas storage facilities, the hundreds of communities that sit above or beside them, and gas customers who depend on the storage system staying intact. The bill gave them a federal safety floor for a type of facility that, until then, had no binding national rules, plus funding for research on detecting leaks by smell.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near gas storage facilities

how_it_helps.text: Directed the Department of Transportation to prescribe strong minimum federal safety standards for underground gas storage facilities within 180 days of enactment, covering operating, abandoned, idled, and plugged wells, including integrity plans, assessments, and emergency plans.

Required every underground gas storage facility to comply immediately with interim requirements: American Petroleum Institute recommended practices 1171 and 1170 for depleted reservoirs, aquifer reservoirs, and salt caverns, plus the recommendations in the pipeline regulator's February 2, 2016 advisory bulletin.
Let states adopt stricter safety rules than the federal floor for facilities within their borders.
Funded research grants on safer storage and on an odorant additive that makes leaking gas both detectable and nontoxic, and imposed a user fee on operators to pay for the oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Underground gas storage facility operators, who would bear the cost of meeting the safety standards, integrity testing, and emergency planning, plus a user fee for each facility. Some of those costs would likely be passed through to natural gas customers in their bills.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas storage operators and gas customers

drawbacks.text: The interim standards the bill mandated were the industry's own voluntary guidelines, written by the American Petroleum Institute, rather than independently drafted government rules, so the immediate baseline was as strong as the industry had already agreed to make it.

The bill imposed compliance costs and user fees on storage operators, and a separate provision allowed the Transportation Secretary to grant a variance, or exception, from the interim requirements where appropriate.
Fee and compliance costs on operators would likely be passed to natural gas customers through their bills, though the fee was restricted so it could only fund underground gas storage oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gap this bill addressed was real: underground gas storage had no binding federal safety standards before this, and the failure of one California facility had displaced thousands of residents. The costs fall mainly on operators and modestly on gas bills, and the fee structure makes the oversight pay for itself. The main design weakness is that the bill's immediate standards lean on industry-written recommended practices rather than independently developed rules; the permanent standards the Transportation Secretary would have written could have gone further, but never were required by this bill because it never became law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, each sent it to a subcommittee, and neither took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 12, 2016 by Rep. Brad Sherman of California, together with 19 cosponsors, all House Democrats from California's delegation.
On the day of introduction it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
Four days later it was sent to subcommittees in both committees, the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials and the Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Underground gas storage operators came out ahead: they avoided binding federal safety standards, integrity assessments, and user fees for another two years. The federal pipeline regulator later moved on this issue on its own, but this bill's mandatory deadlines and fee funding never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas storage operators, who avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were House Democrats and no House Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; the Republican-led committees that received it took no action after sending it to subcommittee.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed binding safety standards, integrity assessments, emergency planning, and user fees on every storage facility, including abandoned and idled wells. Operators' interest in avoiding those costs ran against the public's interest in facilities that do not fail.

industries.industry: American Petroleum Institute and industry standards bodies
industries.note: The bill made the industry's own voluntary recommended practices, API 1170 and API 1171, the mandatory interim federal standards, turning industry self-regulation into government-enforced law. That raised the safety floor for the public while locking in industry-drafted standards as the official baseline.

industries.industry: Natural gas utilities and pipeline operators
industries.note: Storage facilities are pipeline facilities under the bill, so utilities that operate them would pay compliance costs and fees, likely passed to customers. On the other side, a storage failure like the 2015-16 California leak imposed far larger costs on the industry and its customers.
